knowledge_point.title: Calculating Indefinite Integrals Using Substitution with Inverse Secant

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the integral. Give an exact answer.

$$
\int \frac{14}{|14 x|\sqrt{(14 x)^{2}-1}}\,\mathrm{d}x
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the linear substitution $u=14 x.$ Then

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x}=14,\qquad \mathrm{d}x=(\frac{1}{14})\,\mathrm{d}u.
$$

The substitution factor is positive, so the absolute values satisfy

$$
|u|=|14 x|=14|x|,\qquad \frac{1}{|x|}=\frac{14}{|u|}.
$$

Apply the basic inverse-trigonometric integral:

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{u^{2}-1}}\,\mathrm{d}u=\operatorname{arcsec}{\left(u \right)}+C.
$$

Substitute and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{14}{|14 x|\sqrt{(14 x)^{2}-1}}\,\mathrm{d}x &= 14\int \frac{1}{|14 x|\sqrt{(14 x)^{2}-1}}\,\mathrm{d}x \\  &= 14(\frac{1}{14})\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{u^{2}-1}}\,\mathrm{d}u \\  &= 1\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{u^{2}-1}}\,\mathrm{d}u \\  &= \operatorname{arcsec}{\left(u \right)}+C \\  &= \operatorname{arcsec}{\left(14 x \right)}+C\end{aligned}
$$

This antiderivative applies on either interval where $|14 x|>1$; the constant may differ between those intervals.
